Why

An agent that "knows FFmpeg" still guesses: it assumes a frame rate, picks a codec the container cannot hold, re-encodes a file that only needed a stream copy, and reports "done" without opening the result. This skill takes the guessing out:

  • Real files first. Every job starts with probe.py; the agent decides from the measured duration, fps, resolution, colour and audio layout, not from the file name.
  • Structured tools, not shell strings. Each operation is a script with typed arguments. Nothing runs through a shell; no filter graph is accepted from the caller.
  • A contract the agent can read. contract --json states, for every tool, what it takes, what it writes, which FFmpeg components it needs and how the result is verified. The MCP surface is derived from it.
  • Verification after execution. The result is probed, checked against the destination's spec and, when the picture changed, looked at as a contact sheet.
  • Local first. No cloud, no API keys, no Python dependencies. Optional local transcription is used when a speech engine (Parakeet or a whisper) is installed, never required — by caption.py --transcribe and, since 1.17, by silence.py --transcribe (with --filler, or since 3.6 with --sentence-min-silence / --sentence-margin-tail); both take a transcript you already have instead, and both refuse with the install lines rather than guessing. Both take --engine and --model; FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_ENGINE and FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_MODEL set this machine's defaults (e.g. large-v3-turbo where that whisper.cpp model is installed; without either, auto and base). The engine runs on your machine and the audio is never uploaded; parakeet-mlx, faster-whisper and openai-whisper download their model weights the first time they run (parakeet-mlx's default from Hugging Face).

Paper

The design discipline behind this skill — per-operation verification for AI agents — is written up as a position paper. The paper scores ffmpeg-skill itself as only partially conformant with the discipline it defines.

Kajiyama, S. (2026). What Is Verification-Driven Coding? — A Discipline for Not Trusting Generation. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23720216

Quick start

# 0. FFmpeg itself, once (Ubuntu/Debian shown; macOS and Windows are in the Install table below)
sudo apt install ffmpeg

# 1. install the skill for Claude Code (Cursor: --cursor, Codex: --codex, all three: --all)
npx ffmpeg-skill

# 2. check the machine: ffmpeg, ffprobe and every FFmpeg component the tools need
npx ffmpeg-skill doctor

# 3. (for agent frameworks) read the machine-readable contract
npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json | head -40

Captions from speech (caption.py --transcribe) need one local speech engine, installed separately. pip install faster-whisper is the simplest; the first run downloads its model, and the audio never leaves the machine. Without an engine, everything else works, doctor lists the engine as missing optional, and --transcribe refuses with the install line for each engine it supports.

Already installed? re-run npx ffmpeg-skill to refresh ~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill. Copies are not updated automatically.

doctor's overall ok and a single tool's usable are different signals: ok is false when anything some tool requires is missing, so one missing filter (a plain Homebrew ffmpeg without subtitles, or a build without libvidstab) turns it false even though most tools still run. Check doctor --json's tools field for the per-tool answer, not just ok.

Then talk to your agent:

"Take interview.mp4, keep 0:45–3:10 and 5:00–6:30, and make it exactly 60 seconds for Reels."

The agent runs probe.py, cut.py --segments 0:45-3:10,5:00-6:30, fit.py --duration 60 --aspect 9:16 --fit crop, export.py --preset reels, check.py --platform reels and look.py, then reports "final.mp4: 59.98 s, 1080×1920, 30 fps, AAC stereo" with the contact sheet it inspected.

Deliver to a platform

One command per destination, with the app's own UI taken into account:

python3 $S/render.py talk.mp4 --template tiktok --cues cues.txt

That fills the shipped templates/tiktok.json: 9:16 crop, captions popped word by word above TikTok's description bar and clear of its like column, −14 LUFS, the tiktok export preset, and a check.py --platform tiktok on the file it wrote. The caption size comes from the delivery table, so since 1.17.1 the filled project also states "fit_size": "on": a size nobody asked for shrinks to fit the cue instead of splitting the sentence across two cues. A template that states its own fit_size, and a --brand that states a caption size, still win, and a project with "fit_size": "off" renders the captions 1.17.0 rendered. Templates ship for tiktok, reels, shorts, youtube-shorts, youtube, x, linkedin, facebook, podcast and audiogram; --template all (or a comma-separated list) renders the seven video destinations (tiktok, reels, shorts, youtube, x, linkedin, facebook) from the same edit and writes a <name>_pack.md table of what each one produced. Files land next to the input unless -o says otherwise, and --dry-run shows every planned command rather than a result. render.py --list-templates prints them with their frames, limits and safe zones. Alias spellings work everywhere a platform is named (youtube-shorts = shorts, ig = reels, twitter = x, fb = facebook).

The tools also work on their own, from any shell:

S=~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/scripts
python3 $S/probe.py input.mp4 --compact
python3 $S/fit.py input.mp4 --duration 60 --aspect 9:16 --dry-run    # print the plan, run nothing
python3 $S/export.py input.mp4 --preset reels --json                 # structured result with a probe of the output

On Windows in Git Bash, python3 is only on PATH if Python was installed from the Microsoft Store; a python.org install exposes python (or the py launcher) instead — replace python3 with python above if you see a "command not found". bin/install.js and doctor/contract already handle this for you; only the raw script examples above need it spelled out manually.

More requests and the commands behind them: examples/README.md. To see everything run end-to-end on generated footage: npm run demo (the gallery in docs/demos.md).

How it works

flowchart TD
    U[User request] --> A[AI agent<br/>Claude Code · Cursor · Codex]
    A -->|reads| S[SKILL.md<br/>workflow, request → tool map, report format]
    A -->|runs| T[Structured tool<br/>scripts/<name>.py, typed argparse flags]
    T --> C[Contract<br/>input schema · role · capabilities · verification policy]
    C --> D[Capability detection<br/>doctor: available / missing / unknown]
    D --> F[FFmpeg execution<br/>no shell, stream copy when possible]
    F --> V[Verification<br/>probe · check · look.py contact sheet]
    V --> R[Structured result<br/>--json: status, output, commands, probe]
    R --> A

Over MCP the same tools are reached through a transport that holds no tool table of its own:

flowchart LR
    M[MCP client<br/>Claude Desktop · Cursor · any client] --> P[mcp/server.py<br/>stdio JSON-RPC]
    P -->|tools/list| C[Contract-derived ToolSpecs<br/>names · order · inputSchema]
    P -->|tools/call| T[scripts/<name>.py]
    C -.derived from.-> K[scripts/_contract.py]
    T -.described by.-> K

Names, order and inputSchema in tools/list are translated from each tool's argparse parser at start-up, so a new flag or a new script appears in MCP with no edit to mcp/. A test copies the skill, adds, removes and edits a script, and reads tools/list again to prove it.

Design principles

These are the rules the skill file gives the agent and the code enforces.

  1. Probe first. No tool decides from the file name. probe.py measures duration, fps (with variable-frame-rate detection), resolution, rotation, bit depth, HDR format including Dolby Vision, colour tags and every audio stream before anything is cut.
  2. Lossless when possible. cut.py and loudness.py stream-copy what they do not need to touch (join.py re-encodes so it can crossfade and conform mismatched clips; --copy --transition none joins clips that already match by stream copy). Re-encoding happens only when it must: frame-accurate cuts, filters, format changes, or a keyframe farther than the tolerance.
  3. Plan before render. Every tool takes --dry-run (print the ffmpeg command lines, write nothing; verify ignores it), --plan FILE (the dry run saved as a plan with fingerprinted inputs that render.py FILE executes later, refusing if an input changed; render and verify refuse it), --json (structured result with a probe of the output), --fast (preview quality), --progress (percent and ETA), --timeout (a hung ffmpeg is killed and reported, never waited on forever; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM likewise stops the running ffmpeg, removes its partial output and reports kind: interrupted) and --overwrite (explicit consent before an existing output is replaced). A test runs every tool whose contract says its dry run runs no ffmpeg (ffmpeg_execution: none, plus cut and metadata without their measuring flags) under --dry-run behind a fake ffmpeg and asserts that no ffmpeg call happened and no file appeared; another runs every tool the contract says supports --dry-run (all but verify) behind an ffmpeg that logs each decode, and asserts that no file appeared and that every tool that decoded is one the contract lists as analysis_only.
  4. Machine-readable contract. contract --json describes all 42 tools: input schema generated from the parser, output schema, role, required and conditional FFmpeg capabilities, dry-run support, the verification tools to run afterwards, whether a visual check is required, mutates_input: false. provides lists all 42 by a cross-repository Capability id (ffmpeg-skill.cut, ffmpeg-skill.loudness, ...) for kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS's CapabilityContract.provides — see docs/contract.md.
  5. Contract-derived MCP. mcp/server.py builds its tools/list from the contract. Tool names, order and inputSchema cannot drift from the scripts; a test keeps the two byte-identical.
  6. Capability detection. doctor reads ffmpeg -encoders / -decoders / -filters / -bsfs and reports which of the components the tools need are present on this build (libx264, libass, zscale, loudnorm, xfade, …), before a job fails inside ffmpeg.
  7. Unknown is not missing. When a listing cannot be read (a layout the parser does not know, ffmpeg exiting non-zero) the affected capabilities are unknown: never missing, never silently available. An installed filter is not reported absent; a failed detection is not a pass.
  8. Verify the result. The output is probed, and when the picture changed (captions, overlays, crops, colour, transitions) the agent runs look.py and inspects the PNG. The report is not finished until its Look: line names that image; audio-only jobs say Look: not needed. "Inspects" means the calling agent's own vision, not a feature of this skill: look.py only renders a PNG; nothing in this repository detects faces, products, subjects, or "the interesting part" of a frame or a scene. When a crop or reframe needs to keep a specific part of the frame (fit.py --fit crop --crop-x/-y, see Tools), it is the multimodal agent looking at that PNG and choosing the anchor — a non-visual caller (a script, a CLI user without eyes on the sheet) has to supply that decision itself, and the default is a plain centre crop. Likewise scenes.py --highlights ranks candidate scenes by a measured proxy (--rank-by audio or --rank-by duration), never by content; it is the agent that turns a look at the sheet into a judgement.
  9. One label per report. A finished job is Done:, a failure or a refusal is Failed:, and a partial result is Done: with the shortfall named in Notes: — never a third label such as Done (partially):.
  10. Keep originals. No tool overwrites its input. Outputs are new files named <input>_<operation>.<ext> unless told otherwise, and a test hashes every input after the run.

Tools

42 public tools, all Python 3.10+ standard library, all with --help, --dry-run, --json, --plan FILE (a dry run written as a plan render.py executes later), non-zero exit and a reason on stderr on failure. --json-brief (1.11.0) prints the same result document trimmed to what a caller acts on — status, output, verified, a compact summary of the output probe, the tool's own keys and the command count instead of the command lines — for roughly a third of the bytes; --json itself is unchanged. Every re-encoding tool except export.py, render.py and batch.py (a preset or the project decides there) takes --codec h264|hevc|av1|prores and --quality N (1.8) and, with export.py, --hw/--no-hw (Apple VideoToolbox on Apple Silicon, opt-in; see doctor below), and every time flag takes seconds, mm:ss, hh:mm:ss.fff or SMPTE hh:mm:ss:ff with an optional @fps suffix (1.9).

Analysis and inspection

Tool What it does
probe.py Duration, fps (+ VFR detection), resolution, codecs, bit depth, HDR format incl. Dolby Vision (hdr for a real PQ/HLG/DV transfer only, bt2020_or_hdr also for BT.2020 SDR), colour space, rotation, every audio stream; --analyze flags Log footage
scenes.py Scene changes, audio peaks, highlight proposals (--rank-by audio loudest, or --rank-by duration longest — both proxies, not "best") and a per-scene sheet; cut list for cut.py --segments; --beats measures the music's beat grid (tempo, beat times, confidence); --shots classifies each shot static/pan/motion by measured optical flow; --audio-peaks lists per-second dBFS; --speech reports a speech-vs-music ratio, not a classification
look.py Contact sheet, single frames, side-by-side comparison as PNG so the agent can see what it made; --safe NAME shades the zones a platform's own UI covers; --guides title,action,4:3 outlines the broadcast safe areas (on the PNG only)

Editing

Tool What it does
cut.py In/out or multi-segment cuts, lossless -c copy first, re-encode fallback, --accurate for frame-exact video and sample-exact audio, --smart for a frame-exact H.264 cut that re-encodes only the partial GOPs at the cut points (matched to the source, verified against its packets and frames) and copies the rest, an SDR HEVC source re-encodes as HEVC (--no-keep-hevc for x264), a single .mp4/.mov copy keeps its edit list, so the picture starts at --start unless a keyframe lands later (start_snapped then says so; --no-edit-list for 2.x's shifted start), --vfr-guard to choose the VFR check (sampled by default); reports precision; --snap beats moves the in/out points onto a measured beat, or refuses when there is no measurable pulse ; --remove A-B,... drops ranges and keeps the rest
join.py Concatenate clips with xfade transitions, normalising size, fps, sample rate and channel layout (the widest clip's, or --channels); audio-only inputs are joined as audio; --list parts.txt reads generated segments (TTS lines) and checks every one first — missing, empty or unreadable parts are all named in one refusal, or skipped and reported with --on-missing skip ; --copy --transition none joins clips with matching streams by stream copy, measured afterwards, and refuses a mismatch by name
silence.py Detect and remove dead air (jump cuts) with a margin around speech (--margin, 0.2 s each side); list or export the cut list, or a source-to-output time map (--timemap, JSON or CSV); reports the level at every cut and warns where one may land in a breath or a word's tail; --filler also removes filler words, but only where a speech engine timed them; --speech-aware keeps a breath inside a sentence and cuts only at sentence-boundary pauses, composing with --filler through the same keep_ranges(); --margin-lead / --margin-tail keep different amounts before and after speech, and with word timings --sentence-min-silence / --sentence-margin-tail give the pause after a sentence end (the transcript's punctuation) its own floor and tail
fit.py Fit to a duration (pitch-preserving speed change or trim, smooth slow-mo) and/or aspect ratio (pad, crop or --fit blur's blurred, darkened fill, with --crop-x/--crop-y to keep an off-centre subject) and/or exact --width/--height; rotate 90/180/270, flip h/v; force constant fps
crop.py Crop to an exact pixel rectangle (--x --y --width --height) — distinct from fit.py --fit crop, which crops to an aspect ratio it computes itself
cropdetect.py Measure existing black letterbox/pillarbox bars and report the crop.py-ready rectangle that removes them — analysis only, writes no file; --motion-centre reports the per-second motion centroid instead, for a 9:16 reframe — report only, the calling agent picks the crop, no auto-reframing
deinterlace.py Deinterlace interlaced source footage (yadif), --mode frame/field, --parity
denoise.py Reduce video noise/grain (hqdn3d), --strength low/medium/high or individual spatial/temporal overrides
redact.py Blur, pixelate, or (--mode delogo) interpolate away an exact pixel rectangle for the whole clip. The box is given: nothing here finds a face, a plate or a logo, and delogo is a border blend, not inpainting
sphere.py Extract a flat rectilinear viewport from a 360/spherical video (--yaw --pitch --roll --h-fov --v-fov); no subject tracking, only the aim you give it
straighten.py Rotate by an arbitrary angle for horizon correction (--degrees, --fit crop/pad) — distinct from fit.py --rotate's exact 90-degree turns
insert.py Turn a still image into a silent, fixed-duration video clip (title card, end slate) at an exact frame size / fps, with an optional Ken Burns zoom/pan
background.py Generate a solid-colour or two-colour gradient clip at an exact size/duration — no input file; --transparent writes a fully transparent canvas (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG or VP9 with alpha) to draw graphics on
reverse.py Reverse playback (video and, unless --no-audio, audio)
stabilize.py Two-pass motion stabilisation (vidstabdetect/vidstabtransform)
sequence.py Numbered (frame_%04d.png) or glob-matched still images into a video
waveform.py Render an audio track as a waveform or spectrum visualization video (showwaves/showspectrum) — for audio-only inputs with no picture worth showing; --image puts the visualisation over a still plate (an audiogram), with --platform, --title and burnt-in captions
freeze.py Hold a frame for N seconds (--at, --hold, --mode insert/extend) — an end-card hold or a comedic beat
pad.py Add black/silent padding at the start and/or end of the timeline (--start, --end) — distinct from fit.py --fit pad's per-frame letterbox bars
speedramp.py Step through different constant speeds across a clip via --segment START-END:FACTOR (repeatable) — distinct from fit.py's single whole-clip speed factor
loop.py Repeat a clip --times N or to a target --duration — for background loops and filling a fixed slot length; --crossfade smooths the seam, --boomerang plays it forward then backward
broll.py Cut away to a B-roll clip over the A-roll for a window (--insert B --at T --duration D, repeatable) and come back; A's length and audio untouched by default
metadata.py Write container chapter markers from a TIME TITLE text file and title/artist/comment tags, every stream copied bit for bit; --auto-chapters proposes the markers from measured pauses and scene cuts and names them Chapter N for you to rename
grid.py Composite --colsx--rows clips into one grid, each cell letterboxed and labelled with its filename by default (--label none to skip)

Audio

Tool What it does
audio.py Voice clean-up chain at three strengths (--voice light|medium|strong), FFT denoise, typed compressor / limiter / gate, music bed with sidechain ducking (--duck-amount/-threshold/-attack/-release), a never-ducked effects bed (--effects), --stereo-widen, fades, 5.1 → stereo, track replacement, extraction (-o out.wav), --audio-stream N, a tempo change that keeps the pitch (--tempo, atempo stages in 0.5–2.0) and an exact length in samples (--length-samples), resampling (--sample-rate) and one channel by index (--channel N), each read back from the output
sync.py Offset between two recordings by audio cross-correlation (1 ms, pure Python), clock-drift correction; aligned video or audio out (audio-to-audio only — no lip-sync/face detection); a third or later camera is an additional more_sources positional (sync.py REF A B ...), the second positional itself keeps its name
loudness.py Two-pass EBU R128 loudnorm to −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP or any target (--lra for the range), video stream-copied; the written file is measured again and re-encoded until it meets --tp (lossy encoders overshoot); --measure-only; --versions streaming,ebu-r128,broadcast-jp (or LUFS/TP pairs) writes one file per target from one master, each measured after and listed in versions (output is null), verified only when every version met its own target

Picture

Tool What it does
caption.py Burn SRT/ASS with font, size, colour, outline, position; build SRT from timed plain text; wraps to the safe area — with --platform, the destination's own left/right safe zone, which since 1.17.2 is also what the burnt ASS states as its side margins — with a phrase-aware breaker (--wrap phrase|measured) and --max-lines/--min-duration/--offset; --mode mux takes a repeated --srt file:lang for several language-tagged, toggleable tracks in one file; picks a font by script for non-Latin text (--lang); animated and word-by-word karaoke timed to the speech energy or real word timings; --fit-size shrinks the size until a cue fits --max-lines instead of splitting the sentence (on by default on the delivery-template path since 1.17.1, where the size comes from the platform table); says caption text unchanged when it burned the cues exactly as given; optional local transcription
overlay.py Logos, watermarks and titles with position, time range, opacity, fades; --platform NAME keeps them clear of that destination's UI; --video for picture-in-picture, --chromakey for green-screen compositing, --place to lay ranges of a layer at chosen times; --keep-alpha composites onto a transparent canvas or alpha clip and writes the result with its alpha; a VP9 layer with alpha keeps its transparency
graphics.py Lower-thirds, title cards, chapter chips, progress bars, countdowns, corner bugs, social stickers, opening hook cards and meme captions drawn by FFmpeg from a brand kit; --platform NAME keeps them inside that destination's safe zone; --text-render routes shaping scripts through libass and --emoji-assets composites colour emoji; --keep-alpha renders a template on a transparent canvas as a per-element alpha layer
color.py HDR10 / HLG / Dolby Vision → SDR BT.709 tone mapping, DV layer stripping, 3D LUT (.cube), colour-tag rewriting, typed primary correction (exposure/contrast/saturation/gamma/white balance/lift-gain/levels/curves); --keep-alpha grades an alpha clip and keeps its alpha, checked frame by frame; --legalize bt709|ebu-r103: a legal-range clamp after the 4:2:0 conversion, measured on the written file

Delivery

Tool What it does
export.py Presets youtube, youtube4k, reels, tiktok, shorts, linkedin, facebook, x, youtube-hdr (HEVC Main10, source HDR tags kept), youtube-av1, prores, dnxhr-lb/sq/hq/hqx/444, the alpha masters prores4444/prores4444xq/qtrle/vp9-alpha/hap-alpha (alpha read back), key-fill (a switcher's fill + key pair), h265, gif, copy, all tagged BT.709 unless they carry HDR or are an editing master (prores, dnxhr-*: the source's tags kept, codec, profile and pixel format read back) (a BT.601-matrix or RGB source is converted to BT.709, not relabelled); --normalize meets the platform's loudness in the same call (render.py turns it on by default for platform presets) ; --max-mb MB fits the file under a size limit by a two-pass encode and measures it ; --preset copy --repair remuxes a damaged file (timestamps regenerated, corrupt packets dropped) and counts the errors before and after
proxy.py Small, low-bitrate proxy for downstream AI analysis/preview/editing decisions — resize by --width/--scale, proxy-grade --quality (default 30), --fps, --no-audio; not a delivery preset
check.py PASS / WARN / FAIL against YouTube, Shorts, Reels, TikTok, X, LinkedIn, Facebook, broadcast and podcast specs, from the same delivery table the export presets and templates read (podcast also reports chapter markers and channel count), with the fix for each failure and a format / judgement kind per row; a length or file size over the table's upload limit is a WARN marked basis: guidance (platforms change these, the uploader checks the current one), while --max-duration / --max-mb state the caller's own limit and FAIL when a --platform is named (with none, an over-length is WARN like every judgement row); --content adds black-frame, frozen-frame, silence, short audio-dropout, single-frame-flash and flat-first-frame rows ; --compare REF measures SSIM/PSNR against a reference, and with --expect-changed SPAN|none fails when the picture changed outside the spans the caller declared; --levels bt709|ebu-r103 counts the luma and chroma samples outside the broadcast legal range, per clip and per window, with min/max Y/U/V; --expect-identity checks that the file is the one a run reported writing (output_identity)
report.py Single-file HTML delivery report: before/after sheets, media facts, loudness, compliance, the commands run; --pack renders a social pack table

Orchestration

Tool What it does
render.py Render a whole edit from a declarative project.json (clips, transitions, captions, overlays including the social sticker/hook/meme graphics and a picture-in-picture or chroma-keyed video layer sized for the final frame, music and stem levels, loudness, export, chapter markers, check); --init, --dry-run, --stop-after, --cache DIR/--from STAGE (reuse the stages that did not change); the captions block takes the fit-size policy (fit_size, min_size, fit_size_scope) and the run reports the caption stage's counts as caption; --template NAME INPUT renders a shipped delivery template (--template all writes the whole social pack plus its table); --export-timeline edit.fcpxml|.edl|.otio (2.1) writes the cut as an editor timeline for Final Cut, DaVinci Resolve or Premiere instead of rendering it — clips, speed, dissolves, the music bed and chapter markers carry over, and not_exported names what stays behind
batch.py Apply a step recipe or a project to a folder with a content-hash cache; --watch; --jobs N processes several files at once under one shared --timeout
multicam.py Align any number of cameras and recorders by audio (with drift correction) and cut between them from a switch list; --switch energy auto-cuts to whichever camera is loudest at that moment instead of a hand-built list (audio level as a stand-in for who is talking: there is no speaker identification, so it needs each speaker on their own camera's mic), with --min-shot (minimum shot length) and --edl (write a plain START-END cut list, not a CMX EDL; for Premiere/Resolve use --write-project then render.py --export-timeline)
verify.py Run the toolchain on real device files and report PASS / FAIL per step

Not tools, but part of the surface: mcp/server.py (the MCP transport) and scripts/_contract.py (contract --json, doctor). Per-flag reference for every tool: references/scripts.md.

Audio is a first-class input

WAV, FLAC, MP3, M4A/AAC, OGG and Opus go through probe, cut, join, silence, loudness, audio, sync and check --platform podcast with the same commands as video. The output extension picks the codec: -o out.wav writes PCM, -o out.flac FLAC, -o out.mp3 MP3, -o out.m4a AAC.

  • Extraction. An audio extension on a video input drops the picture: audio.py talk.mp4 -o talk.wav, or --voice -o talk.m4a to clean it on the way. --audio-stream N picks a track; probe lists them under audio_streams.
  • Join. join.py intro.wav episode.m4a outro.wav -o full.flac resamples every clip to one rate and channel layout and crossfades them (--transition none for a butt join). Audio and video inputs cannot be mixed in one join.
  • Sample-accurate trims. cut.py talk.wav --start 1.2345 --end 2.3456 --accurate trims at the sample; the JSON reports precision (packet for a stream copy, sample for PCM / FLAC, codec_frame when a lossy encoder frames the audio again, frame for video) and the measured duration_error_ms. A .wav never receives compressed packets.
  • Typed dynamics. audio.py --compress --comp-threshold -20 --comp-ratio 4, --limit --limit-ceiling -1, --gate --gate-threshold -45. Each flag is one documented option of FFmpeg's acompressor, alimiter or agate, range-checked before ffmpeg runs; no filter string is accepted from the caller.
  • Loudness. loudness.py talk.wav -I -16 --tp -1.5 -o talk.m4a for podcast levels; check.py talk.m4a --platform podcast measures LUFS and true peak and reports the chapter markers and channel count.

Picture tools (fit, caption, overlay, graphics, color, export, look) refuse an audio file with "input has no video stream" instead of inventing a picture. scenes.py measures an audio file (audio_only: true, one scene): --beats, --audio-peaks, --speech and --highlights run on the sound, and --sheet / --shots are refused.

Built for agents

What is SPEC?

SPEC (Self-Producing Execution Contract) is the name this project's author, kajisho5, gave the pattern the tool layer is built on: each tool's input_schema — the part of its contract that has to track the CLI exactly, flag for flag — is never hand-authored side by side with the code. It is derived, at run time, from the one thing that has to be correct for the CLI to work at all: the script's own argparse parser.

Concretely, scripts/_contract.py's _capture_parser() imports every tool script and intercepts its parse_args() call to get the live, fully-built parser object — flags, types, choices, defaults, required/positional, mutually exclusive groups, all of it. input_schema is built straight from that object. (The rest of a ToolSpec — role, capabilities, inputs, outputs, output_schema — comes from a hand-authored table, TOOL_META, since those facts aren't things a parser can express; only input_schema is parser-derived.)

  • The contract's input_schema for every tool is generated from the live parser directly.
  • SKILL.md is two-tier (1.11.0): the file the agent loads every session keeps the workflow, the request→script table and one line per gotcha; the long-form detail lives in references/gotchas.md and the other references/ files, read only when a job needs it.
  • The MCP server (mcp/server.py) carries no schema of its own; tools/list is translated straight from the contract, input_schema included.
  • The docs (docs/contract.md's field reference, this README's tool table) describe the same shape. tests/test_contract.py runs on every CI run and fails the build if any of them drift out of sync with what the code actually does — it catches drift, it doesn't fix it for you.

So adding a flag to a script's argparse block updates input_schema and the MCP tool definition with no second edit, and a docs page or TOOL_META entry that falls behind fails CI rather than drifting silently. There is no separate input_schema file to forget to update.

Machine-readable contract

npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json            # or: python3 scripts/_contract.py --json
npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json --static   # without environment detection

The contract is generated from the code that runs, not maintained beside it. For each of the 42 tools (ffmpeg-skill/<name>) it states:

Field Meaning
input_schema generated from the tool's argparse parser: properties, types, enums, defaults, required, positional order, mutually exclusive groups
output_schema what --json prints: status, output, commands, probe, output_identity ({size, mtime_ns} of the file written, on every tool but probe), plus tool-specific fields (precision, checks, offset_seconds, …)
role analysis, analysis_and_execution, execution or verification
capabilities the FFmpeg encoders, filters and bitstream filters the tool always needs, and the ones needed only for a flag or input
supports_dry_run, supports_json, supports_json_brief measured by the tests, not declared
verification which tools to run on the output afterwards (probe, check, look)
requires_visual_verification the picture changed; inspect the contact sheet
audio_only, video_required whether an audio-only input is accepted or refused
mutates_input always false
idempotency_hint bit_exact, content_equivalent, cached or environment_dependent

Next to the tool list the document carries a top-level deprecated list (since 1.10): what the next major removes, since when, the replacement and the surface it lives on. It is empty in 3.0.0: Python 3.9 and FFmpeg 5.x, the two 2.x entries, moved to removed with what 2.0 removed, and docs/contract.md "What 2.0 changed" and "What 3.0 changed" are written from that.

contract_version (2.0) is separate from the skill version, so a consumer can pin the shape and read the version for provenance. The document also states the invocation mapping (structured arguments → argv), the JSON shapes for success and failure ({"status": "failed", "error": {"kind": "input | ffmpeg | output | missing_tool | timeout | verification | interrupted", "message": …}}; a refusal adds error.reason, a stable code such as output_exists or plan_inputs_changed, and error.details, the facts behind it; warnings, fallbacks and skipped steps a run decided on its own are in diagnostics), and that no tool runs a shell or executes anything other than the named script, ffmpeg and ffprobe. Field-by-field reference: docs/contract.md.

MCP

{"mcpServers": {"ffmpeg-skill": {"command": "python3", "args": ["/Users/you/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/mcp/server.py"]}}}

On Windows, python3 is only on PATH if Python was installed from the Microsoft Store; a python.org install exposes python (or the py launcher) instead — if your MCP client reports the server failed to start, change "command" above to "python" (or the full path from where python).

mcp/server.py is a stdio JSON-RPC transport with no tool table of its own. tools/list is derived from the contract at start-up, in contract order, with inputSchema translated from each tool's input_schema. By default it lists only the core 12 (render, look, caption, export, check, fit, cut, audio, loudness, graphics, silence, probe) so a client doesn't pay context for 30 schemas it rarely calls directly; set FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1 to list all 42. Every tool, listed or not, is callable through tools/call, which maps structured arguments to argv and runs the named script; a raw argv form is accepted for compatibility and marked non-canonical. python3 mcp/server.py --list prints the tools; --call probe '{"inputs": ["a.mp4"]}' runs one from the shell.

No inputSchema lists json or progress: they are transport flags the server sets itself, not tool arguments (2.0; 1.x listed them unless FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_LEAN=1). A client that still sends them is not refused.

A structured value is never read as an option: one that starts with - (overlay text -50%) is passed as --flag=value, and positionals that start with - follow --. probe, check and cropdetect are annotated readOnlyHint and write no file over MCP (their plan is refused, structured or in a raw argv); every other tool is destructiveHint, because with overwrite it replaces an existing file. See docs/contract.md § MCP relationship.

The server also advertises a prompts capability: five canned workflow recipes an agent can ask for by name instead of composing the individual tool calls itself — reel, podcast, multicam, delivery_check, hdr. prompts/list returns each one's name, description and arguments; prompts/get {name, arguments} fills the matching template and returns one text message naming the actual command lines to run and what to check afterward. These are recipes, not new tool calls — every command line a prompt names is one tools/call (or the CLI) can already run.

Capability detection

npx ffmpeg-skill doctor          # human-readable
npx ffmpeg-skill doctor --json   # available / missing / missing_optional / unknown / detection / errors / tools / gpu_encoders / ffmpeg_security

doctor reads ffmpeg -encoders, -decoders, -filters and -bsfs and resolves every capability the contract declares against this machine's build. Three states per capability: available, missing, unknown. Exit 0 when everything required is available, 1 when something required is missing, 2 when nothing is proven missing but a required capability is unknown. With detection on (the default), contract --json carries the same lists under capabilities. doctor also reports fonts: the default drawtext family, and fonts.scripts — one available/missing/unknown per writing system (ja, zh, ko, ar, he, hi, bn, ta, th, lo, ru, el, latin) with the file it would use — so "can this machine render Korean captions" is answered before the job, not after. doctor --json's tools field folds that down to one answer per tool — {"caption": {"usable": "no", "missing": ["filter:subtitles"], "fix": "..."}, ...} — so "is doctor overall ok" and "can I run caption.py on this machine" are answered separately: a plain Homebrew ffmpeg is ok for tools that don't need subtitles/drawtext/zscale, while caption's own usable is "no".

doctor --json's gpu_encoders reports which GPU-backed encoders (nvenc, videotoolbox, qsv, vaapi, amf) this ffmpeg build was compiled with — read from -encoders alone, so it proves the capability shipped, not that the GPU/driver on this machine will actually accept a job (that needs a real encode, which doctor's introspection never runs). It never affects ok or any tool's usable. The one GPU path a tool uses is Apple VideoToolbox, opt-in: --hw on every re-encoding tool (h264/hevc/prores on the GPU, AV1 stays on SVT-AV1), FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1 to make it this machine's default for everything except export.py's delivery presets (those take --hw explicitly, or render.py --hw for a whole project). It runs only on Apple Silicon and never by default, except on a build with no libx264/libx265 (an LGPL ffmpeg that has only h264_videotoolbox/hevc_videotoolbox): there it is the only encoder, so every re-encoding tool and export.py's presets use it without --hw, the result says hw.source: "auto", and doctor lists the missing x264/x265 under covered_by instead of calling the tools unusable (--no-hw still asks for the CPU). It falls back to the CPU encoder — reported in the result's hw.fallback/hw.notes — only when VideoToolbox itself refuses a job (any other ffmpeg failure is reported as it happened, not retried); every result names the encoder that actually ran (batch.py, which encodes nothing itself: each results row), and a GPU encode adds a notes line that its quality is not CRF-equivalent. Measured on an M4 Max, 2–7× faster than x264/x265 medium; at matched SSIM (tests/bench_vt.py) 1.1–2.9× the bytes on SDR and 1.9–3.5× on HDR, which is why it is a flag and not the default (docs/design-decisions.md). doctor --json's hw says whether this machine can run it (platform_ok) and whether it is the default here (default_on).

doctor also compares the FFmpeg version with a small, dated table of high-severity FFmpeg CVEs (doctor --json's ffmpeg_security; source ffmpeg.org/security.html, checked 2026-10-22). ffmpeg-skill does not ship FFmpeg, so a decoder bug in the build you have stays yours until you upgrade it. When the version is older than the first upstream release on its branch that carries a fix (today: CVE-2026-8461, the MagicYUV decoder heap write, fixed in 8.0.3, 8.1.2 and 9.0), doctor prints one warning: line on stderr with the update command and lists it under ffmpeg_security.warnings. It is advice, never a failure: ok, each tool's usable and the exit code do not change. A distribution package (Ubuntu 8.0.1-3ubuntu2, Debian +deb13u1) may carry the fix as a backport under the old version number, so the line says the build is older than the fix, not that it is vulnerable. A version it cannot read (a git snapshot such as N-12345-g…) gets no warning, and nothing is fetched: the table ships with the skill.

Gotchas and best practices

The short list for humans. The agent-facing version, with the reasoning, is the "Things that look right but are wrong" and "Gotchas" sections of SKILL.md.

  • Variable frame rate (phone and screen recordings). probe.py flags it; every re-encoding tool conforms to a constant rate automatically. cut.py samples the frame timing before a copy and switches to frame-accurate mode when it is variable or too short to judge, because copy-cuts on VFR land on the wrong frame (--vfr-guard average restores 2.x's rule, re-encoding whenever the nominal and average rates differ; --vfr-guard off keeps the copy). Choose the rate yourself with fit.py input.mp4 --fps 30 when the measured average is odd.
  • Lossless cuts snap to keyframes. A stream-copy cut can start up to one GOP earlier than asked. cut.py re-encodes when the snap exceeds 0.5 s (--tolerance changes the limit). For a strictly lossless file pass --tolerance -1 (plus --vfr-guard off on a variable-frame-rate source), and expect the cut to land on the nearest earlier keyframe; the JSON result lists them under nearest_keyframes. A --segments join can still be re-cut: open-GOP video, a later segment of B-frame .mp4/.mov video that starts between keyframes (start it on a keyframe, or write .mkv), or a join that fails its check. A single .mp4/.mov copy keeps its edit list by default (since 3.0.0), so the picture starts where asked: the keyframe's pre-roll is stored but hidden by an MP4 edit list, which a player that ignores edit lists shows (--no-edit-list starts the file at the keyframe instead).
  • Frame-exact without re-encoding the whole cut (H.264). cut.py --smart re-encodes only from each cut point to the next keyframe and copies the GOPs between, matched to the source's profile, level, pixel format, B-frame depth and colour tags. It checks the result against the source (frame grid, copied packets, decoded frames). A source it cannot match (HEVC, 10-bit, interlaced, VFR, open GOPs) is re-encoded in full, and smart.reason says why. probe.py --keyframes-near T shows where the keyframes are.
  • HDR stays HDR. When the probe reports HDR (HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision, BT.2020), the tools keep it rather than flatten it. Convert deliberately with color.py --to-sdr before H.264 deliverables or LUT work. export.py platform presets are SDR and warn on HDR input.
  • Loudness targets. −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP for YouTube and social platforms (the loudness.py default), -I -16 --tp -1.5 for podcasts, -I -23 for broadcast. A clip measured at −40 LUFS or below is room tone, not content; raising it raises the noise. Check true peak as well as LUFS: check.py file --platform podcast measures both.
  • Alpha is kept only when asked, and a lost alpha is not verified. The re-encoding tools write opaque H.264 by default. On a source whose alpha is used (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG, VP9 with alpha), color.py, graphics.py and overlay.py take --keep-alpha (ProRes 4444 by default, --alpha-codec qtrle|png|vp9, --alpha-mode straight|premultiplied) and read the alpha back; without it the result says verified: false with a failing alpha step, and --drop-alpha records that an opaque output is wanted. background.py --transparent makes the canvas to draw graphics on.
  • Broadcast legal levels are measured, not assumed. check.py final.mxf --levels ebu-r103 (or bt709) counts every luma and chroma sample outside the legal range and FAILs when one frame has more than 1 % out (--levels-tolerance); the JSON levels adds min/max Y/U/V per --levels-window. color.py --correct --legalize ebu-r103 clamps after the 4:2:0 conversion and measures what the encode left: a lossy encoder can push a few samples around a clamped edge back out, so the result says how many.
  • Frame changes first, text second. Captions and overlays burned before a crop or resize end up off-frame. Reframe, then caption.
  • Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 discards 70 % of the width. fit.py --fit crop centres by default; pass --crop-x/--crop-y toward the subject, or pad with --fit pad --pad-fill blur. Look at the contact sheet before deciding.
  • Phrase-aware caption breaking (1.16). caption.py/graphics.py --wrap phrase (the default) never breaks inside a word or on the wrong side of a hyphen, never leaves a lone digit, kana or punctuation pair on a line, prefers Japanese sentence ends and particles over a mid-word break, and never ends a line on an article or preposition. All four are penalties over break positions that already fit, so no line is widened and the line count never changes; --wrap measured restores 1.15's width-only wrap. The text itself is never rewritten or shortened. Since 1.16.1 a Thai run and a katakana word are never broken inside (Thai writes no space inside a phrase and there is no dictionary: the break goes where you put a space or |), and a line wider than the safe width is reported as overlong with the fix named.
  • Caption size fitted to the cue (1.17, reachable from the templates since 1.17.1). At a platform caption size a line holds about six em, so an ordinary sentence needs four lines and --max-lines 2 used to cut it into consecutive cues — half the sentence arriving late. caption.py --fit-size (default auto) walks the size down until every cue fits, before laying the cues out, with a legibility floor of 4.5 % of the frame height (--min-size, default 13 ASS units). An explicit --size or a brand.json size is a statement about the look and is never overridden — which in 1.17.0 also silenced the fitter on every render.py --template run, since a template fills the size from the platform table; 1.17.1 marks that size as the default it is ("fit_size": "on" in the filled project), so the type shrinks and no cue is split. --fit-size off restores that earlier behaviour byte for byte, and the caption text is still never rewritten to make it fit.
  • Beat-synced cuts (1.17). scenes.py --beats reports the measured grid — tempo, beat times, and a confidence built from how far the winning autocorrelation lag stands above the others and how many onsets land on it. cut.py --snap beats (and a "snap" block in a render.py project) moves in/out points to the nearest beat within --snap-tolerance — and only onto the grid points a measured onset actually marks, never onto the regular grid's continuation through a passage with no music in it. Below --min-confidence it refuses: a cut point may move to a measured beat and may not appear from one, so speech and ambience get an honest "no steady pulse here" instead of an invented grid. A music bed is measured as it is delivered, WAV/FLAC/MP3 with no picture; on a synthetic click track at 90 and 120 BPM every beat is within 1 ms (WAV/FLAC) or 9 ms (MP3) of its click, tests/test_analysis.py holds it to 20 ms.
  • Filler words (1.17). silence.py --filler --words transcript.json removes "um" and "uh" through the same cut graph the silences use. Never without measured word timings — there is no heuristic that finds an "um" without them that would not also cut real speech — and like, tipo and cioè are deliberately not in the built-in lists, because a discourse marker is a content word. Built-in lists since 2.19: English, Japanese, Korean, Chinese, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Russian and Turkish; any other language takes --filler-words FILE. Whisper stays optional: --transcribe with no engine installed refuses and names the five installs.
  • Throughput (1.17). batch.py --jobs N runs several files at once, capped at min(N, cpu_count, 8) and sharing one --timeout budget rather than one per item; the per-item table keeps its order. render.py --cache DIR reuses stages whose inputs and arguments did not change, so swapping an export preset re-runs export only. The cache is opt-in with no default directory, and the ffmpeg, skill and contract versions are part of every key, so a cache is never reused across them.
  • Audiogram (1.16). waveform.py --image cover.png (or render.py --template audiogram) puts the waveform over a still plate for an episode that has no picture, with --platform for the frame, --title and burnt-in captions. The image is a local file you give: nothing is fetched and no cover art is ever invented.
  • Emoji in captions and titles (1.15). caption.py/graphics.py --emoji-assets DIR composites a PNG per emoji (Twemoji naming, 1f389.png, or Noto's emoji_u1f389.png) on top of the text, because drawtext cannot load a colour emoji font at all and an installed one does not prove libass will draw it in colour — doctor --json's fonts.emoji answers that from a render probe. Without assets the result's emoji.mode says which of three things happened: color when this build's libass draws the colour glyph (also for --emoji mono on such a build, with a warning), mono when it draws a monochrome one, and none when the emoji are left out of the text: with an emoji_not_drawn warning when that happened because nothing here draws the glyph, and with only an info line when --emoji none asked for it (and a graphics.py title that is nothing but emoji is refused). Nothing is ever downloaded.
  • Indic and Thai text shaped correctly in titles and lower-thirds (1.15). graphics.py renders Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Thai and Lao through libass automatically (text_renderer: "ass"), because drawtext never reorders matras or re-clusters marks; Arabic and Hebrew were already correct on a fribidi build. --text-render drawtext with such a script is refused, never rendered wrongly.
  • Non-Latin text picks a font by script (1.12). Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, Cyrillic and Greek cues, titles and overlays resolve a font file that covers them automatically, and a machine with no such font fails the job (kind: input) instead of rendering boxes. doctor --json's fonts.scripts says which languages this machine can render; --lang ja|ko disambiguates Han-only text, and --lang zh-TW (or zh-HK, zh-Hant) picks a Traditional Chinese face (2.19); an explicit --font/--font-file is always kept.
  • Silence detection finds nothing? The default threshold is −35 dBFS. The tool prints a hint with the track's measured level; raise the threshold (silence.py --threshold -25) or shorten --min-silence.
  • Sync results carry a confidence. Below 0.3, or an offset near the edge of the analysis window, is probably wrong: enlarge --analyze-seconds or find a clap. Recordings over ten minutes from separate devices need sync.py --fix-drift.
  • Outputs are never overwritten silently. An existing output path is refused (kind: input, error.reason: output_exists, before anything runs); pass --overwrite where a replacement is intended.
  • Nothing happens silently. A refusal names its error.reason and error.details; a stale output lock taken over, a run without a lock, a plan input nobody could fingerprint, a fallback (an odd-sized frame scaled to even, a substituted font, libaom for SVT-AV1), a skipped step and every warning are recorded in diagnostics and on stderr (codes: json_output.diagnostic_codes); tools that draw text name the font they drew with (font_used). A refused plan and a lock takeover also append a line to an audit log (<plan>.audit.jsonl, or render.py --audit-log FILE). A degraded or partial result says so: render.py's verified is every stage's, an unmeasured loudness or a report section that could not be built is a failing verification step, export.py reports trimmed, multicam.py's cuts name the camera rendered, and batch.py rows carry the failing step's error, verified, and a row for every input after Ctrl-C.
  • Long masters need a longer --timeout. The default is 1800 s per ffmpeg call, which is there to catch a hang. A full re-encode of an hour of 1080p at the default preset ran past it on a 4-core machine (see A one-hour recording). Pass --timeout 0 or a larger value, or --fast. Analysis and stream-copy cuts are far below it.
  • Long chains belong in a plan. Three hand-chained re-encodes lose quality and are hard to change; render.py runs the whole edit from one JSON file, and --dry-run shows every ffmpeg command before anything is written.

FAQ

Can I pass raw ffmpeg arguments, or a filter_complex?

Each operation is a script whose flags are its argparse parser, and that parser is what contract --json and the MCP inputSchema are built from. CI fails the build when those drift from the scripts. A caller-supplied filter graph, -vf string, or other ffmpeg option is not an argument any script accepts. doctor reads ffmpeg -filters (and -encoders, -bsfs) and reports a filter a tool needs before a job runs into it. MCP does accept an argv array, and that array is the named script's own CLI flags, still bound to that script: the script's flags, never an ffmpeg command line and never a shell.

Why 42 tools? Isn't that overkill?

One tool per job, because each job promises something different, and the tool measures that promise after the run. loudness.py re-measures integrated loudness and true peak. cut.py reports how far a cut snapped to a keyframe. silence.py returns the ranges it kept. export.py checks the preset's maximum length. A value a tool cannot read fails that step as not_measured; it does not pass. One tool with a mode flag would need as large a schema, and its checks would be vaguer.

An agent does not read 42 schemas. Over MCP, tools/list advertises the core 12 (bold below). The other 30 are called by name through tools/call when a job needs one, and FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1 lists all 42. The groups are the ones in Tools.

Group MCP default / all Tools
Analysis and inspection 2 / 3 probe, look, scenes
Editing 3 / 24 cut, fit, silence, join, crop, cropdetect, deinterlace, denoise, redact, sphere, straighten, insert, background, reverse, stabilize, sequence, waveform, freeze, pad, speedramp, loop, broll, metadata, grid
Audio 2 / 3 audio, loudness, sync
Picture 2 / 4 caption, graphics, overlay, color
Delivery 2 / 4 export, check, proxy, report
Orchestration 1 / 4 render, batch, multicam, verify
Total 12 / 42

Without the other 30, an agent writes raw ffmpeg for those jobs, and a mistake there often still exits 0:

  • stabilize.py runs vidstab in two passes, and the second pass needs the first pass's transforms file.
  • color.py builds the HDR-to-SDR chain. With a wrong colour tag the run still finishes, and the picture comes out washed out.
  • join.py puts transitions between clips that differ in size, frame rate or audio layout. Done by hand, those clips have to be normalised first or xfade fails.
  • sync.py and multicam.py find the offset between two recordings by audio cross-correlation. No ffmpeg filter measures it.

Every command a tool records as run is in its --json commands (batch.py lists none of its steps' commands, and a measurement pass is listed only where the tool records it), shell-quoted so it can be pasted and run again, except a line that names a file the tool wrote for the run and removed when it exited (such as a concat list, an ffmetadata file, a drawtext text file, a two-pass log or a stage's intermediate), and --dry-run on a writing tool prints the commands without writing the output (some dry runs still run a measurement, and verify.py ignores --dry-run: see below). In the 100-prompt agent eval (1.17.0, Tested on real footage) the agent made no raw ffmpeg calls and reported no false successes.

What does verified check, and what can it not tell me?

verified covers what can be measured from the file. Each tool measures its output again: the probe (the file opens, its duration, codecs, size and frame rate) and the tool's own promise. For example, loudness and true peak after loudness.py or export.py, the length against the asked one, and for cut.py, join.py and export.py the stream count, where picture and sound end, and whether both ends of every stream decode. check.py grades a file against a platform's limits. A value that cannot be read fails its step as not_measured; it does not pass.

It cannot tell you whether the result looks or sounds right, and the result says so: every writing tool lists the properties it did not measure in unverified. Examples are picture_content (what is in the frame), subject_framing after a reframe, rendered_placement and legibility of captions and titles, grade_look after a colour conversion, removed_span_content after a silence cut (whether a removed span held speech), mix_balance and lip_sync. For those, look at frames with look.py (a contact sheet, or --safe for a platform's UI zones) and listen where the result points you. silence.py lists the level at every cut, and cut_warnings names the cuts that may have landed in a breath or a word's tail.

Are silence removal and captions stable?

They are the most used tools here, and they are tested on every pull request and every push to main on Linux, macOS and Windows, with FFmpeg 6.1 to 9. On 20 test files with known gaps, silence.py missed none and left at most 1 ms of silence (see Tested on real footage). A cut keeps --margin seconds of air on each side, 0.2 s by default; raise it to 0.3 s for a speaker who trails off. --speech-aware keeps the short breaths inside a sentence. Filler words are removed only from measured word timings (--words or a local --transcribe), never guessed. --timemap writes where each kept and removed range sits in the source and the output, for re-timing subtitles. If --threshold is set high enough to cut into a breath or a weak word ending, the result warns at that cut.

caption.py burns SRT/ASS or muxes them as soft tracks, fits the size to the platform's safe area, and picks a font that covers the script (Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Thai, Hindi and others). It needs FFmpeg's subtitles filter (libass); doctor reports whether this build has it. Placement and legibility are listed as unverified, so look at a contact sheet before delivering. Speech-to-text runs on a local engine you install; its first run may download a model.

How well does HDR to SDR work, and what should I watch for?

color.py --to-sdr converts PQ (HDR10), HLG and iPhone Dolby Vision 8.4 to SDR BT.709 with real tone mapping (zscale and tonemap, hable by default; mobius, reinhard, clip, linear and gamma with --tonemap). BT.2020 footage on an SDR transfer gets a gamut conversion only. Watch for four things:

  • It needs zscale (libzimg). The plain Homebrew ffmpeg lacks it, so use ffmpeg-full (keg-only: see Install for putting it on PATH); doctor reports whether it is there.
  • --peak (default 1000 nits) is the PQ source's brightest level, the one that becomes SDR white: set it to how bright the source was mastered (its MaxCLL or mastering peak). Too high dims the picture; too low clips the highlights. HLG always peaks at 1000 nits, so --peak does not apply to it.
  • Tone mapping is a judgement, and the result says so (grade_look in unverified). Compare frames with look.py, and try another --tonemap if skin or skies look off.
  • An HDR source that only needs to play everywhere may not need converting at all. --strip-dovi removes the Dolby Vision layer from an iPhone clip, keeping its HLG picture, with a stream copy.

How does ffmpeg-skill compare with Remotion?

ffmpeg-skill edits footage you already have, on this machine, with FFmpeg tools whose flags are a machine-readable contract (contract --json). Remotion renders a video from React components. They complement each other: this repository does not call Remotion, and a file Remotion writes is an ordinary input (probe.py, cut.py, fit.py, export.py, check.py). remotion-ffmpeg-skill joins the two. It measures the footage with this repo, draws the graphics in Remotion from those measurements, and checks and delivers the result with this repo again. Install both (npx ffmpeg-skill, then npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill). As with the other skills, the dependency runs one way: it calls these tools, and nothing here calls it. HyperFrames renders a video from HTML and is the same kind of neighbour: a file it writes is an ordinary input too.

Does it validate the filter graph before running?

No. --dry-run prints the ffmpeg command a writing tool would run and does not start ffmpeg, so ffmpeg never parses that filter graph. ffprobe still runs when the tool probes an input that exists. Unless --overwrite is passed, an existing output is refused (kind: input) before ffmpeg. An output that is the same file as an input is refused either way. No media file is written, and verified is false; --plan FILE does write the plan JSON. A path that is not on disk yet is not measured: the probe is a stub (0×0, duration 0), so a number taken from it is not a measurement. The measuring tools (probe, check, sync, multicam, scenes, cropdetect, report, silence, loudness, stabilize) still run their measurements; only the artifact is skipped, and silence with --transcribe (with --filler or a sentence flag) also runs the speech engine, which may download a model. overlay measures the lines of a multi-line --text with one drawtext on a generated frame on FFmpeg 8.0, 8.0.1 and 8.1.0, where it draws them one by one. metadata with --auto-chapters and cut with --snap beats decode the input for their measurement, and render and batch run each stage or step as its own dry run, so a measuring stage measures an input that exists. verify accepts --dry-run and ignores it: its steps run, and its document says dry_run: false. --plan FILE is that dry run written down — the planned argv, the command lines, and a fingerprint of each existing input (size, plus a sha256 of the first and last 8 MiB). render.py and verify.py refuse --plan. render.py FILE runs a plan only when those fingerprints still match (a mismatch is refused with each input's expected and actual fingerprint in error.details, and logged to <plan>.audit.jsonl), by running the tool again with the planned argv, not by executing the recorded ffmpeg lines; --dry-run on that run only prints them. doctor reports whether the filters, encoders and bitstream filters the contract names are in this build (ffmpeg -filters, -encoders, -bsfs) and which fonts are installed. A name in that listing is not a check of the graph this command would build, and a listed GPU encoder is not a successful encode.

Can it remove burned-in subtitles or logos?

A rectangle you already know, sitting still for the whole clip, can be filled from the picture around it with redact.py --mode delogo (ffmpeg's delogo filter). That is a 1 px border blend. It is not inpainting: a logo that moves, or burned-in subtitles whose position changes, is out of scope. The same known box can be obscured instead, with --mode blur or --mode pixelate. None of the three finds the box. delogo also needs the box at least 1 px inside the frame, and it only interpolates 8-bit YUV, so an HDR or 10-bit source is refused until color.py --to-sdr.

Does it auto-track faces or subjects for reframing?

fit.py --fit crop centres the crop unless you pass --crop-x and --crop-y. crop.py cuts the rectangle you pass. cropdetect.py measures letterbox bars, and --motion-centre reports where motion sat each second; it writes no file and picks no crop. sphere.py points a 360 view where you aim it. look.py writes a contact sheet. Nothing in this repository detects a face, a product or a subject. Choosing what to keep in frame is the caller's.

Does it encode on the GPU?

The encode path a tool will actually take is Apple VideoToolbox, for h264, hevc and prores, and only on Apple Silicon. --hw asks for it on that call. FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1 makes it the default for every re-encoding tool except export.py's delivery presets, which take --hw on their own (or render.py --hw for a whole project). AV1 stays on SVT-AV1. nvenc, QSV, VAAPI and AMF are reported by doctor --json's gpu_encoders when the ffmpeg build was compiled with them, and no tool encodes with them. One build is the exception to opt-in: with no libx264 and no libx265, and with h264_videotoolbox or hevc_videotoolbox, those encodes use VideoToolbox without --hw and the result says hw.source is "auto". --no-hw still asks for the CPU encoder. A VideoToolbox job the hardware refuses is re-encoded on the CPU and the result says so (hw.fallback).

FFmpeg compatibility

The tools need FFmpeg 6.1 or later and Python 3.10 or later (standard library only). 3.0.0 removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9: every tool refuses an ffmpeg/ffprobe whose version reads as older than 6.1 (kind: missing_tool, error.reason: ffmpeg_unsupported; a git build whose version is not a release number is not refused), and doctor lists an unsupported FFmpeg or Python under unsupported with ok: false. What CI actually exercises on every pull request is FFmpeg 6.1 (Ubuntu 24.04 apt), 7.1 (Debian trixie apt), 8.x (macOS Homebrew), 9.x (Windows gyan.dev) and 8.0.1 (Ubuntu 26.04 apt), on Python 3.10 and 3.13 (the two ends of the supported range). The capability parser has been run against the listings of these builds:

FFmpeg -filters row layout Source
6.1.1 three flag characters: ..C acompressor A->A Ubuntu 24.04 apt, captured
7.1.x same as 6.x Debian trixie apt in a CI container (plus a constructed fixture in tests/)
8.1.2 two flag characters: TS aap AA->A, three-character legend, ------ separator Homebrew on the macOS CI runner, captured
9.0.1 same as 8.x, CRLF gyan.dev build on the Windows CI runner, captured

FFmpeg 8 shortened the flag column of ffmpeg -filters. A parser anchored on the old width matches nothing on FFmpeg 8 and, if "nothing matched" is read as "nothing installed", reports every filter missing; that is what 0.9.0 did on macOS and Windows. Since 0.9.1 rows are recognised by their io-spec token (A->A, AA->A, |->V, N->N), so the flag width, the legend and the separator do not matter, and a listing that still cannot be read yields unknown rather than missing. The captured listings live in tests/fixtures/ with their provenance; CI uploads each runner's listing and doctor --json as an artifact so a new layout is visible before it bites.

A one-hour recording

Measured at 2.17.0 (2026-10-25) on one 60-minute 1080p30 H.264 file (4.3 GB, AAC mono 48 kHz, synthetic testsrc2 picture and a tone). The machine was a 4-vCPU Xeon at 2.1 GHz with FFmpeg 6.1.1 on Linux, and each tool ran alone. The analysis rows read the whole hour (silence.py, scenes.py and check.py report 3600 s). The edit and export rows used 10-minute segments cut from it with stream copy, and the last row is the whole hour.

Step Wall time Note
probe.py 0.3 s
silence.py --list 14 s one audio decode
loudness.py --measure-only 66 s
look.py (contact sheet) 97 s
scenes.py 241 s
check.py --platform youtube --content 308 s the rows, dropouts included, cover the full hour
cut.py, a 10-minute stream-copy segment 2.4–4.4 s no re-encode
join.py, two 10-minute segments 624 s join.py re-encodes by default, so it can crossfade and conform (--copy does not, for clips that match)
export.py --preset youtube, a 10-minute segment 514 s about 1.2× real time at the default medium preset
export.py --preset youtube --fast, the same segment 162 s about 3.7× real time at veryfast
export.py --preset youtube, the whole hour killed at 1802 s kind: timeout at the default --timeout of 1800 s (below)

A full-length re-encode of an hour does not fit in the default --timeout. The limit is 1800 s per ffmpeg call. On this machine export.py --preset youtube on the whole hour was killed at 1802 s with kind: timeout (exit 124), and nothing was written. At the 10-minute segment's rate it would have needed about 50 minutes. A whole-hour join.py would land at the limit. The error message names the fix. For a long master, pass --timeout 0 (no limit) or a larger value, or --fast, which at the measured rate takes about 16 minutes for the hour. Analysis tools and stream-copy cuts stay far below the limit.
